title: Pool-barrier rules by state and territory: where to check
audience: Pool and spa technicians, cleaners and supervisors who need to know which authority to ask about a pool barrier in each state and territory
learningOutcomes: Explain why barrier rules differ between states and territories.
Find the barrier authority for the job's state or territory and record the source, the page date and the status
Record a certificate as sighted without interpreting it as proof of current compliance
Refer certification, repair, licence and other questions the sources do not settle instead of answering them.

instruction.heading: Australia-wide, with no single rule
instruction.body: Pool barrier rules are not one national rule. Each state and territory sets its own requirements through its own laws, and councils or other authorities enforce them. Who inspects differs by place: councils and registered inspectors in NSW, licensed pool safety inspectors in Queensland, councils in South Australia, and pool safety advisers in the Northern Territory. The national framework includes the National Construction Code, which contains the Building Code of Australia, and the barrier standards AS 1926.1 and AS 1926.2, which the ACT page names as AS 1926.1-2012 and AS 1926.2-2007. This lesson names those framework items only.

instruction.heading: How to use the table
instruction.body: For each job, do four things. First, confirm the state or territory and the local council for the address. Second, find the authority named for that jurisdiction on its official page, and record the page address and the date you read it. Third, ask the owner for any certificate or notice, and record its type, its issuer and its date as sighted. Do not treat it as proof of current compliance. Never apply one state's rule to another. All checks in this pass were made on 3 November 2026.

instruction.heading: Western Australia (checked for the December 2025 guide; partly checked for initial inspections)
instruction.body: The December 2025 WA guide, Rules for Pools and Spas, supersedes the 2016 edition. The WA publication page (first published 15 November 2024, last updated 26 November 2024) links to it. The guide says that water deeper than 30 cm brings a pool under the barrier rule. It sets a barrier height of 1.2 m or more on the non-poolside, a gap of no more than 100 mm under the barrier and under a gate, and a latch release at least 1500 mm above the ground on the non-poolside under its first option. It caps the horizontal gap between vertical members at 100 mm. It says local governments inspect barriers at intervals of no more than four years and are the permit authorities, and that a building permit is generally needed before a swimming or spa pool is built or installed. The WA Government page on initial barrier inspections (first published 13 November 2024, updated 19 November 2024) covers new private pools and existing pools that have never been inspected. It does not say who may carry out those inspections, gives no deadline and does not name the inspecting authority. The WA Department of Health page (last reviewed 12 December 2023) says the Health (Aquatic Facilities) Regulations 2007 cover aquatic facilities open to the public and leave out domestic pools. Checked for the guide's barrier figures as read in this pass (check the PDF before reliance); partly checked for the initial-inspection page and the Health regulations point.

instruction.heading: New South Wales (checked, owner page)
instruction.body: The NSW Government owner obligations page (last updated 16 March 2026) says pools that can be filled with water to more than 30 cm are covered. A barrier must reach 1.2 m or more, with height taken from the finished surface, and the gap at the bottom must not exceed 10 cm. Vertical bars may not be more than 10 cm apart, and horizontal climbable bars must be at least 90 cm apart. Gates must stay shut and open outward, not toward the water. They must shut by themselves whatever position they were released from, and they must latch on their own. Registration on the Swimming Pool Register does not show compliance. Councils or registered inspectors can issue a certificate of compliance, which remains in effect for 3 years, or a certificate of non-compliance. Checked for the authority, certificate and measurement points listed on the page. The page is not consistent on the depth wording for portable pools, so confirm the threshold with the council.

instruction.heading: Queensland (partly checked)
instruction.body: The QBCC pool safety inspector page (last reviewed and published 31 August 2021, with a fee change stated for 1 July 2026) says a licensed inspector under the scheme may inspect a pool and then issue a certificate or a non-conformity notice. Such an inspector may also make minor repairs, such as adjusting a latch or hinge or removing a climbable object, and may erect or repair parts of a barrier, but the page limits that barrier work to a total length of 5 metres and to 6 posts at most. A technician who is not a licensed inspector should not act as one. Partly checked, because the page is dated 2021. The current licence scope must be checked on the QBCC site before reliance.

instruction.heading: Victoria (checked for inspectors; partly checked for repairs)
instruction.body: The Building and Plumbing Commission page on pool and spa safety barrier inspections (updated 30 June 2026) says that building surveyors, building inspectors and pool inspectors who are registered do these checks. The inspector issues the Form 23 barrier compliance certificate. Where doubt remains about the fence, an inspector does not issue it. After a notice, the owner has 60 days to comply, and the inspector must form an opinion within 60 days of the inspection. The Victorian Building Authority consumer page on pool safety barriers (no date shown) says that pools and spas deeper than 300 mm need a compliant barrier, that owners must keep barriers working, and that a permit may be needed to alter an existing barrier, with advice to check with the council or building surveyor. Checked for the inspector role and the certificate; partly checked for the repair and permit point.

instruction.heading: South Australia (checked for council inspections; partly checked for the licensing point)
instruction.body: Practice Direction 8 on council swimming pool safety inspections (no version date shown) says councils must inspect all pools and pool safety features completed in a reporting year. The timeframe is two weeks from the point at which a council learns that the works are finished. The inspections are carried out by councils, not by pool service technicians. The SA Consumer and Business Services building licence FAQs (November 2025) list works on a pool or spa as an example of domestic building work, which needs a building work contractor licence. Checked for council inspections; partly checked for the licensing point.

instruction.heading: Tasmania (checked; page dated 8 December 2023)
instruction.body: The Consumer, Building and Occupational Services page on pool safety barriers (last updated 8 December 2023) says barriers are required for pools and spas with water 300 mm or more deep that were installed from 1994 onward. Covers over a pool or spa do not count as barriers. Licensed builders install barriers under the oversight of a licensed building surveyor, and a licensed building surveyor checks inflatable or relocatable pool barriers before the pool is filled. For pools installed before 1994, the page recommends fitting a barrier but does not require one. Checked, on a page dated 2023.

instruction.heading: Australian Capital Territory (checked)
instruction.body: The ACT Planning page on home swimming pool safety reforms (no date shown) says the scheme began on 1 May 2024 with a four-year transition. It covers pools and spas deeper than 30 cm at residential buildings. From 1 May 2028, compliant barriers and barrier compliance certificates become mandatory, and certificates issued from then are valid for five years. Authorised persons issue barrier compliance certificates; licensed building surveyors are authorised automatically, and others are authorised under a 2024 appointment instrument. The page cites AS 1926.1-2012 and AS 1926.2-2007. Checked.

instruction.heading: Northern Territory (partly checked)
instruction.body: The NT Government page on pool fencing and barrier safety standards (no date shown) covers residential properties under 1.8 hectares. It says pools installed after 1 January 2003 need a compliance certificate in the owner's name, issued after a pool safety adviser inspects the barrier. Older pools have obligations that depend on whether the property has been sold or leased since 1 January 2003. The page applies to pools that can be filled to 30 cm or more at the deepest point and names the Swimming Pool Safety Act 2004. Partly checked, because the page is undated and the full text was not read.

instruction.heading: What this table does not cover
instruction.body: Pool chemical licences, dangerous goods thresholds for pool chemical storage, electrical licences for pool equipment, public-pool registration, and water discharge rules are not covered in this table for any jurisdiction. Use “Dosing systems and chlorine-gas prevention” for chemical handling, “Electrical, mechanical and confined-space boundaries” for electrical and plant boundaries, and “Water conservation and environmental release” for discharge.

procedure: Confirm the state or territory and the local council for the site address.
Find the barrier authority for that jurisdiction in this lesson, then open its official page and record the page address and the date you read it.
Ask the owner for any certificate, notice or register entry. Record its type, issuer and date as sighted, and write no compliance opinion.
If the status is only partly established, or the page is out of date, tell the responsible person and direct the owner to the council or the local permit body.
Record which rule source you used, its date and its status on the job record.
Refer any certification, repair, licence or public-pool question to the responsible person or the authority. Do not answer it yourself.

workedExamples.situation: A house in Hobart. The owner says the pool was installed in 1990 and asks whether the barrier is compliant. You are booked for a clean.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you say, and what do you record?
workedExamples.reasoning: The Tasmanian page (last updated 8 December 2023) applies its barrier statement to pools installed from 1994 onward and recommends that owners of older pools add a barrier. You do not say whether the barrier complies. You tell the owner that a licensed building surveyor or the local council can advise on the barrier. You record the owner's question, the page used and its date, the status (checked, dated 2023), and that no compliance statement was made.

workedExamples.situation: A house in Perth. The owner shows you a barrier certificate from a few years ago and asks whether the pool meets the current rules. The pool was built before 2016.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How do you record the certificate, and what do you tell the owner?
workedExamples.reasoning: You record the certificate type, its issuer and its date as sighted. You do not interpret it as current compliance. The WA guide used here is the December 2025 edition, which supersedes the 2016 edition, so the owner should ask the local government, which the guide names as the body that inspects and permits barriers, whether the current rules affect this pool. This lesson does not confirm current compliance.

workedExamples.situation: A Brisbane owner has a non-conformity notice from a pool safety inspector and asks you to confirm the barrier is now fixed.
workedExamples.reasoning: A non-conformity notice is a record that a licensed inspector issues under the QBCC scheme. You are not licensed as a pool safety inspector and cannot confirm the item is closed. You do not describe the barrier as compliant.

equipmentAndPpe: Job record with fields for the state or territory, the authority, the page address and the date read
Owner's certificate or notice, if one is shown, for sighting only
Council or permit authority contact details, from the job file
Closed footwear with grip, and PPE as set by {{business:safety.required_ppe}}

commonErrors.error: Applying the WA figures or the WA rules to a job in another state.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only the authority and rule source for the job's own state or territory.

commonErrors.error: Treating an old certificate as proof that the barrier is compliant today.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the certificate as sighted, with its date and issuer, and refer the question to the authority.

commonErrors.error: Quoting a barrier measurement from memory or from another state's page.
commonErrors.prevention: Quote only what the job's official page states, with its address and date.

commonErrors.error: Signing or issuing a certificate of any kind.
commonErrors.prevention: Only the authority or an authorised inspector issues barrier certificates. Refer the request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This lesson does not give authority to inspect for legal compliance, issue or sign any certificate, or repair a pool safety barrier. The inspectors and authorities named here decide certification.

The national framework names (National Construction Code and the Building Code of Australia, AS 1926.1 and AS 1926.2) are named here only. The NCC 2022 Volume Two Part H7 page is read for its barrier requirement, and the ACT page names the standards.

The WA example (Health (Aquatic Facilities) Regulations 2007) applies in Western Australia only. The Department of Health page says it covers aquatic facilities open to the public and leaves out domestic pools.
Page dates matter. Several pages used here are dated 2021 or undated. Check the page on the day of the job where the job depends on it.

qualityStandard: The job record names the state or territory, the authority, the page address and the date read
Any point not established for the jurisdiction is recorded as unresolved, not assumed.
No record or statement treats a certificate as current compliance, and no certificate is signed or issued by the learner
Certification, repair and licence questions are referred to the named authority or the responsible person
documentationEvidence: Authority table entry used, with page address and date read
Certificate sighting record, with type, issuer and date, and a note that no compliance opinion was given
Referral record: who was told, when, and which authority was named
summary: Barrier rules are set by each state and territory and by councils. There is no single Australian rule to apply.
Find the authority for the job's jurisdiction, record the source and date, and record any point that is unresolved.
A certificate is recorded as sighted. It is not a current compliance statement, and the learner does not sign one.
Refer certification, repair, licence and public-pool questions rather than answering them.

knowledgeChecks.question: You are booked for a job in a state that this lesson does not describe in detail. What should you do?
options: Apply the Western Australian figures, because they are the most detailed and easiest to find for any state
Find the official authority for that state or territory, record the page and its date, or mark the point as unresolved
Use the rules from the nearest state, since they are similar to yours and easy to check for the job
Assume the national framework sets the same figures everywhere in the country and across all the states

knowledgeChecks.question: Which statement about the national framework names in this lesson is correct?
options: They are named here only; their text was not read, so their content is not set out here
They have been read and confirmed for this course in full by the learner today
They set one rule that applies in every state and territory in Australia and the islands
They replace the authority in each state and territory, so no local authority is needed

knowledgeChecks.question: A homeowner shows you a certificate of compliance issued by a registered swimming pool inspector in New South Wales. What is the correct step?
options: Tell the owner the barrier is certified for life, since the certificate was issued by a registered inspector
Record that you sighted it, with its type, date and issuer, and do not treat it as a current compliance statement
Sign a new certificate yourself, since you are on site with the owner and the pool today and can see the barrier
Remove the certificate from the file, since it is out of date and no longer useful for the owner or the council
